question: What is a computer network?
gold_answer: A computer network is a set of devices (often referred to as nodes) connected by communication links. A node can be a computer printer or any other device capable of sending and/or receiving data generated by other nodes on the network. More simply it is two or more computers linked together for the purpose of sharing information resources or both.

question: What are the five components of a data communications system?
gold_answer: A data communications system has five components: Message (the information to be communicated) Sender (the device that sends the message) Receiver (the device that receives the message) Transmission medium (the physical path by which the message travels) and Protocol (the set of rules governing data communications).

question: What are the four fundamental characteristics of an effective data communications system?
gold_answer: The four fundamental characteristics are: Delivery (the system must deliver data to the correct destination) Accuracy (the system must deliver data accurately without alteration) Timeliness (the system must deliver data in a timely manner without unacceptable delay) and Jitter (variation in the packet arrival time which must be controlled especially for audio and video).

question: What is data communication and how does it differ from a computer network?
gold_answer: Data communication is the exchange of data between two devices via some form of transmission medium such as a wire cable. Telecommunication means communication at a distance and data refers to information presented in a form agreed upon by the parties. Computer networks are the highways on which data travels — they exist so that data communications can occur between devices.

question: Describe the three modes of data flow (transmission modes) between two devices.
gold_answer: Communication between two devices can be Simplex (data flows in one direction only e.g. from mainframe to monitor) Half-Duplex (data flows in both directions but not simultaneously — one device transmits at a time e.g. walkie-talkie) and Full-Duplex (data flows in both directions simultaneously e.g. telephone conversation).

question: What is distributed processing and what are its advantages?
gold_answer: Distributed processing is a network feature where a task is divided among multiple computers rather than a single powerful computer handling all processing. Each computer handles a subset of the process. Advantages include: Security Distributed Databases Faster problem solving Security through redundancy and Collaborative processing.

question: What are the benefits of a computer network?
gold_answer: The benefits of a computer network include: Information sharing (authorised users can access and share data databases and group projects) Hardware sharing (one device such as a printer or scanner connected to the network can be shared by many users) Software sharing (a program installed on the server can be accessed by all users from a single location) and Collaborative environment (users can work together on group projects by combining the power and capabilities of diverse equipment).

question: What are the risks of network computing?
gold_answer: The security of a computer network is challenged every day by: Equipment malfunctions (which may be caused by natural disasters such as floods storms or fires and electrical disturbances) System failures Computer hackers and Virus attacks.

question: What three criteria must a computer network meet to be considered effective and efficient?
gold_answer: To be considered effective and efficient a computer network must meet three most important criteria: Performance (measured using transit time and response time and depending on number of users type of transmission medium hardware and software) Reliability (measured by accuracy of delivery frequency of failure recovery time after failure and network readiness in the event of catastrophe) and Security (protecting data from unauthorised access and viruses).

question: What is a communications channel and what is the difference between physical and wireless transmission media?
gold_answer: To transfer data from one computer to another requires a link through which the data can be transmitted — this link is known as the communications channel. Sending data through the channel requires transmission media which may be either physical (tangible cable-based) or wireless. Physical media include twisted-pair cable coaxial cable fibre-optic cable and ISDN lines. Wireless media include microwave systems satellite systems cellular technology and infrared technology.

question: Describe the four types of physical transmission media used in computer networks.
gold_answer: Twisted-pair cable consists of two independently insulated wires twisted around each other and is the least expensive type used in many telephone systems. Coaxial cable consists of an insulated centre wire grounded by a shield of braided wire and is the primary type used by the cable television industry. Fibre-optic cable contains hundreds of clear fiberglass or plastic fibres that can carry more data and is lighter and less susceptible to interference but is fragile and expensive. ISDN line is a special digital telephone line that transmits and receives information at very high speeds.

question: What are the two most common types of networks and what is the primary difference between them?
gold_answer: The two most common types of networks are Local Area Networks (LANs) and Wide Area Networks (WANs). The primary difference is that a LAN is generally confined to a limited geographical area such as a building or office whereas a WAN covers a large geographical area. Most WANs are made up of several connected LANs.

question: Distinguish between a LAN and a WAN and list the types of WANs.
gold_answer: A Local Area Network (LAN) spans a small area such as a building or office where software applications and resources are stored on a file server and print servers enable multiple users to share the same printer. A Wide Area Network (WAN) spans a large geographical area and includes several types: Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) Public Access Network (PAN) Value Added Network (VAN) and Virtual Private Network (VPN).

question: What is an Intranet and how does it differ from an Extranet?
gold_answer: An Intranet is a private LAN designed for use by everyone within an organisation. It might consist of an internal e-mail system a message board and one or more web site portals containing company news forms and personnel information and access is restricted by a firewall. An Extranet is a network that connects people within a company with people outside the company within a secure password-protected network that can be accessed from anywhere.

question: What are the three properties used to categorise or classify networks?
gold_answer: Networks are usually classified using three properties: Protocol (the agreed-on rules for transmitting data) Architecture (the way a network is designed and built — peer-to-peer or client/server) and Topology (the way computers and peripherals are configured — bus star ring mesh or hybrid).

question: What is a network protocol and what features does it determine?
gold_answer: A protocol is an agreed-on set of rules and procedures for transmitting data between two or more devices. Features determined by the protocol include: how the sending device indicates it has finished sending the message how the receiving device indicates it has received the message and the type of error checking to be used. Most networks use Ethernet while on the Internet the major protocol is TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol).

question: What are the two major types of network architecture and how do they differ?
gold_answer: Network architecture refers to the way a network is designed and built. The two major types are: Peer-to-peer architecture where computers connect with each other in a workgroup to share files printers and Internet access — used to connect a small number of computers. Client/server architecture where information is sent from a client computer to a server which then relays the information back to the client or to other computers on the network — suited for larger networks.

question: Describe the four main network topologies.
gold_answer: Network topology refers to the way computers and peripherals are configured to form networks. Bus topology: all computers are linked by a single line of cable. Star topology: multiple computers and peripheral devices are linked to a central computer called a host. Ring topology: each computer or workstation is connected to two other computers with the entire network forming a circle. Mesh topology: every device is connected to every other device providing multiple redundant paths. Hybrid topology combines different layout types to meet specific needs.

question: What is a Network Interface Card (NIC) and what is its role in connecting a node to a network?
gold_answer: The NIC is a board installed in a computer or network device. In many computers it is built into the main board. One end is accessible on the outside of the workstation via a connector for attachment to communications media and it may also be a separate card inserted into an expansion slot. Imprinted on every NIC is a hardware address known as the Media Access Control (MAC) address. MAC addresses (also called Physical Addresses) are unique for every host device and nodes are attached to networks through communications media via the NIC.

question: What are the five main networking hardware devices and what does each do?
gold_answer: The five main networking devices are: Repeaters (also called amplifiers) — electronic devices that receive weakened signals and amplify and resend them along the network. Hubs/Switches — electronic devices with a number of ports used in a LAN to link groups of computers. Routers — electronic devices used to ensure messages are sent to their intended destinations. Bridges — hardware and/or software that allows communication between two similar networks. Gateways — hardware and/or software that allows communications between dissimilar networks.

question: Explain how a repeater works and why it is necessary in a network.
gold_answer: A common problem in networking is that electrical signals weaken as they travel through copper wire due to electrical resistance. This limits the length of cable that can be used. A repeater overcomes this limit when there is a need to connect two computers at a larger distance. A repeater is connected to two cable segments — any electrical signal reaching it from one segment is amplified and retransmitted to the other segment.

question: What is a hub and what is its major limitation?
gold_answer: The hub was introduced when new Ethernet technologies brought new cable types that could not fulfil the physical characteristics required by the original physical bus Ethernet. The hub's major function is to replicate data it receives from one device attached to it to all other devices. However using hubs can contribute to congestion on an Ethernet network because all ports share the same collision domain. Hub networks are usually limited to a maximum of about ten hosts before performance deteriorates significantly.

question: What is network segmentation and which devices are used to achieve it?
gold_answer: Network segmentation is the process of breaking up one large network into a number of smaller ones to improve performance. As the number of hosts on a hub network increases network performance deteriorates so segmentation becomes necessary. Network segmentation is achieved with devices like Switches Routers and Bridges. Note that hubs do not segment a network — they only connect hosts on a particular segment together.

question: Compare routers and switches in terms of OSI layer operation broadcast domains and collision domains.
gold_answer: Routers operate at Layer 3 (Network Layer) of the OSI model and by default break up both broadcast domains and collision domains — they provide a separate broadcast domain for each interface. Switches (Layer 2 switches) operate at Layer 2 (Data Link Layer) and break up collision domains by default but do not break up broadcast domains — they create separate collision domains but a single broadcast domain. Switches do not create internetworks while routers do. Switches switch frames from one port to another within a switched network while routers forward packets between different networks.

question: What is a bridge and how does it reduce network traffic?
gold_answer: A bridge is a network device that filters data traffic from one network segment to another. Bridges reduce the amount of traffic on a LAN by dividing it into two network segments. A bridge examines each data frame and passes those known to be within the same LAN segment while forwarding those known to be on the other interconnected segment. Bridges learn which MAC addresses are on which network and develop a learning table (Bridging Table) so subsequent messages can be forwarded to the right network. Bridges operate at the data link layer (Layer 2) of the OSI model.

question: What is a gateway and how does it differ from a router?
gold_answer: A gateway consists of hardware and/or software that allows communications between dissimilar networks. Historically the term gateway was used to refer to a routing device but in the TCP/IP world the term router now describes such a device. Today the term gateway refers to special-purpose devices that perform protocol conversions — they implement application layer conversions of information received from various protocols. Examples include voice gateways that convert speech on analogue phone lines to network protocol data and video gateways that convert video from digital phone lines to LAN protocol data.

question: What is a firewall and what is its function in a network?
gold_answer: Firewalls are systems that establish access control policies among networks. They can block information from entering a network or from getting out of that network and they can permit different users to perform different kinds of operations according to the user's authorisations. An intranet's website is typically restricted by a firewall to prevent unauthorised external access.

question: What are the two types of modem (by location) and how does a modem work?
gold_answer: A modem is a device that converts digital data from a terminal or computer to analogue signals used by voice communication networks such as the telephone system and converts audio tones back to digital pulses at the receiving end. The word Modem stands for MOdulator-DEModulator. Internal modems are electronic cards installed in one of the computer's expansion slots. External modems are fully functioning external devices connected to the computer using a serial cable and powered by an external power source. Modems are available in different transmission speeds measured in BPS (bits per second) also called BAUD rate.

question: Given the IP address 195.143.208.133/25 what class is it and what is its default subnet mask?
gold_answer: The address 195.143.208.133 falls in the range 192.0.0.0 to 223.255.255.255 which is a Class C address. The default subnet mask for a Class C address is 255.255.255.0 (or /24 in CIDR notation). The /25 in the given address indicates a custom subnet mask of 255.255.255.128 (11111111.11111111.11111111.10000000 in binary).

question: Given IP address 176.184.238.73/16 what class is it and what is the NetID?
gold_answer: The address 176.184.238.73 falls in the range 128.0.0.0 to 191.255.255.255 making it a Class B address. Since it is a Class B address the NetID is determined by the first 16 bits. In binary: 10110000.10111000.11101110.01001001. Filling the host portion with zeros gives 10110000.10111000.00000000.00000000 which in decimal notation is 176.184.0.0.

question: What is CIDR notation (the /n notation) and what does /16 represent in dotted decimal and bitwise notation?
gold_answer: CIDR stands for Classless Inter-Domain Routing. The /n notation indicates the number of bits in the network (subnet mask) portion of the address. /16 means the first 16 bits are all ones representing the network portion. In dotted decimal notation /16 is 255.255.0.0 and in bitwise notation it is 11111111.11111111.00000000.00000000.

question: For the IP address 176.184.238.73/16 what is the HostID?
gold_answer: Since this is a Class B address with a /16 mask the HostID is determined by the last 16 bits of the IP address. The network portion is 10110000.10111000 (176.184) and the host portion is 11101110.01001001 (238.73). Therefore the HostID is 238.73 and the host address range for this network is 176.184.0.1 to 176.184.255.254.

question: How many subnets and hosts per subnet are created when subnetting 176.184.0.0/16 into /20 subnets?
gold_answer: To create 16 subnets from the /16 block 4 bits are borrowed from the host side (2^4 = 16 subnets) giving a new prefix of /20 with subnet mask 255.255.240.0. Each subnet has 12 host bits remaining supporting 2^12 = 4096 addresses per subnet and 4094 usable host addresses (subtracting network and broadcast addresses). The subnet addresses increment by 16 in the third octet: 176.184.0.0/20 176.184.16.0/20 176.184.32.0/20 and so on up to 176.184.240.0/20.

question: What are the causes of LAN traffic congestion?
gold_answer: Causes of LAN traffic congestion include: Too many hosts in a single broadcast domain Broadcast storm Multicasting Low bandwidth Adding hubs for connectivity to the network and a large amount of ARP or IPX traffic. Note that a switch does not break up broadcast domains — it only creates separate collision domains while the broadcast domain remains shared.

question: Explain the functions of a router in a network.
gold_answer: Routers are used to connect separate networks together and route packets of data between them. The functions of a router include: Packet Switching (forwarding packets from one network to another) Packet filtering (examining packets and deciding whether to forward or discard based on routing rules) Internetwork communication (creating internetworks that allow different networks to communicate) and Path selection (choosing the best path for packets using a routing table). Routers also by default break up both broadcast and collision domains and provide connections to WAN services.

question: What are the different wireless transmission media and what factors determine which medium is selected?
gold_answer: Wireless media include: Microwave system (transmits data via high-frequency radio signals through the atmosphere) Satellite system (receives transmitted signals amplifies them and retransmits them to the appropriate locations) Cellular technology (uses antennae resembling telephone towers to pick up radio signals within a specific cell area) and Infrared technology (transmits data as infrared light waves from one device to another providing wireless links between PCs and peripherals). The type of medium selected is determined by the type of network the size of the network and the cost.

question: What is the Ethernet bus and how does it work?
gold_answer: Ethernet LANs use a bus topology where all stations are connected to a single long cable. Any station can send a signal along the cable which all other stations will receive. Unlike ring topologies the cable does not close a loop. The original Ethernet LANs (physical bus) relied on the physical characteristics of coaxial cable. When new cable types were introduced that could not fulfil those requirements hubs were introduced to simulate the bus characteristics.

question: Explain how a Token Ring network operates.
gold_answer: A token passing ring LAN is a group of computers connected in a loop that uses a token passing access mechanism. A computer wishing to send data must first receive permission by acquiring the token. When it gets control of the network it may transmit a frame. Each frame transmitted on the ring is passed from one computer to the next until it ultimately returns to the initiator of the transmission. This ensures orderly access to the network and prevents collisions.

question: What is hostname to IP address resolution and when is DNS used versus a broadcast?
gold_answer: When two hosts on a network need to communicate they use their hardware (MAC) addresses. If a host knows only the other host's name and not its IP address it must perform hostname to IP address resolution. If the two hosts are on different networks this requires a Domain Name Service (DNS) lookup. If the two hosts are on the same LAN the sending host can send a BROADCAST message to all hosts on the network to request the MAC address corresponding to the known hostname — this is handled by the NetBIOS Name Service (NBNS also known as WINS on Windows systems).

question: What are the common communication protocols used for application-level communication on a network?
gold_answer: Common application-level communication protocols include: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) — used to transmit files between systems. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) — used to transmit e-mail messages. POP (Post Office Protocol) — allows the recipient to retrieve messages from a mail server. HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) — used by web browsers to request and transfer web pages. WAP (Wireless Application Protocol) — enables wireless devices to access the Internet using a client/server network. 802.11 — the protocol standard for wireless LAN technology.

question: What is entrepreneurship according to Stevenson and Jarillo?
gold_answer: According to Stevenson and Jarillo entrepreneurship is fundamentally about pursuing opportunities even without controlling the resources required to exploit them. It involves identifying and acting on a favorable set of circumstances to create value regardless of whether the entrepreneur currently controls all the necessary resources.

question: How did Fred Wilson define entrepreneurship?
gold_answer: Fred Wilson defined entrepreneurship as the art of turning an idea into a business. This definition emphasizes the creative and practical nature of entrepreneurship — it is not just about having ideas but about executing and transforming those ideas into viable operating businesses.

question: What resources do entrepreneurs combine in launching a venture?
gold_answer: Entrepreneurs combine multiple resources in the process of launching and growing a venture including money (financial capital) people (human capital such as employees and partners) strategy (the plan and direction for the business) and business models (the framework that defines how the venture creates and captures value).

question: What are the common reasons people become entrepreneurs?
gold_answer: The most common reasons people become entrepreneurs include the desire to be their own boss (freedom from management control) the desire to pursue their own ideas and innovations the possibility of financial rewards and the desire to escape the frustration of working in conventional employment. Most entrepreneurs are primarily motivated by independence and the opportunity to create something meaningful rather than by money alone.

question: What is the number one characteristic consistently found in successful entrepreneurs?
gold_answer: The number one characteristic consistently found in successful entrepreneurs is passion for their business. Passion drives persistence through setbacks attracts employees and investors and sustains effort over the long-term journey of building a venture.

question: What is execution intelligence and why is it important in entrepreneurship?
gold_answer: Execution intelligence refers to the ability to convert an idea into a viable business. It is arguably the most important entrepreneurial characteristic because having a great idea is not sufficient — the entrepreneur must be able to translate that idea into a working organisation with systems processes and a team. Many ventures fail not from bad ideas but from poor execution.

question: Explain the myth that entrepreneurs are born not made and why it is incorrect.
gold_answer: The myth that entrepreneurs are born not made suggests that entrepreneurial talent is entirely genetic or innate. This is incorrect because entrepreneurial success depends significantly on environment education experiences and deliberate choices rather than on birth. Entrepreneurial skills such as opportunity recognition creativity networking and execution intelligence can be learned developed and improved over time through training mentorship and practice.

question: What is the difference between an entrepreneurial firm and a conservative firm?
gold_answer: An entrepreneurial firm is proactive innovative and willing to take calculated risks to pursue opportunities and drive growth — it has a high level of entrepreneurial intensity. A conservative firm is risk-averse less proactive and tends to preserve the status quo rather than seek new opportunities. Entrepreneurial firms like Starbucks embrace innovation and calculated risk-taking while conservative firms tend to prioritise stability and avoid uncertainty.

question: What are the three types of start-up firms?
gold_answer: The three types of start-up firms are: Salary-substitute firms which are small businesses that provide owners with an income roughly equivalent to what they would earn in conventional employment (e.g. a local hair salon). Lifestyle firms which provide an owner with the ability to pursue a particular lifestyle while also earning a living (e.g. a surf instructor who runs surf lessons). Entrepreneurial firms which bring new ideas products or services to market with the intent to grow create wealth and eventually achieve significant scale. Government-regulated monopolies are NOT a type of start-up firm.

question: What is an entrepreneurial opportunity and what are its four essential qualities?
gold_answer: An entrepreneurial opportunity is a favorable set of circumstances that creates a need for a new product idea or service. The four essential qualities of a true opportunity are: it is Attractive (desirable to customers and the market) Timely (the window of opportunity is open) Durable (it has longevity not just a passing trend) and Anchored in a product service or business that creates or adds value for its buyer or end user. A true opportunity is NOT completely risk-free.

question: What is the difference between an opportunity and an idea?
gold_answer: An idea is an unvalidated thought or concept about a potential business — for example a person thinking of creating a drone delivery service without having researched market feasibility or demand. An opportunity is a validated favorable circumstance that has been assessed for market demand attractiveness and viability. Most ideas are NOT opportunities until they have been rigorously tested against market and feasibility criteria.

question: What are the main approaches to identifying entrepreneurial opportunities?
gold_answer: The main approaches to identifying entrepreneurial opportunities are: Observing trends (economic forces social forces technological advances and political/regulatory changes) Solving problems (identifying persistent challenges people face and designing solutions such as addressing reliance on fossil fuels) and Finding gaps in the marketplace (identifying overlooked or underserved customer groups such as Daisy Rock Guitars designing guitars specifically for female players). Blindly copying competitors is not a legitimate approach to opportunity identification.

question: Give an example of how each major environmental trend can create an entrepreneurial opportunity.
gold_answer: Economic forces: GasBuddy.com was created to help consumers find and save on fuel costs during periods of fuel price volatility. Social forces: Daisy Rock Guitars identified and served female guitar players who were overlooked by mainstream manufacturers — an example of how increasing diversity and changing demographics create opportunities. Technological advances: Digital photography replacing film cameras shows how technological disruption creates entirely new industries. Political and regulatory changes: The No Child Left Behind Act in the US created opportunities for firms like Shakespeare Squared which produces educational materials to help schools meet new standards.

question: What is entrepreneurial alertness and how does prior experience support opportunity recognition?
gold_answer: Entrepreneurial alertness is described as a sixth sense — a unique ability to notice opportunities that others miss. It allows entrepreneurs to identify patterns connections and gaps in the marketplace before others do. Prior experience in an industry or functional area supports opportunity recognition by: helping entrepreneurs spot market niches they understand building domain knowledge that informs what is missing or suboptimal and providing access to professional networks and contacts who share information about gaps and emerging needs.

question: What is the role of weak-tie relationships versus strong-tie relationships in entrepreneurship?
gold_answer: Weak-tie relationships are ties between casual acquaintances or people who interact infrequently — they are especially valuable to entrepreneurs because they expose them to new perspectives diverse ideas and information outside their normal circles. Strong-tie relationships are ties between close friends family and frequent collaborators — they provide support and trust but tend to reinforce existing thinking. Research shows that most entrepreneurs get their best ideas from social and professional contacts including weak ties rather than from close family and friends alone.

question: What is creativity and what are the five stages of the creative process?
gold_answer: Creativity is the capacity to produce novel and useful ideas. The five recognized stages of the creative process in order are: Preparation (researching and immersing oneself in the problem or opportunity) Incubation (allowing the subconscious mind to process the information — the idea gestates) Insight (the eureka moment when a solution or idea crystallises often called Illumination) Evaluation (critically assessing whether the idea is viable and worth pursuing) and Elaboration (developing the idea into a workable form — turning insight into reality). Regulation is NOT one of the five stages.

question: What is brainstorming and what conditions make it most effective?
gold_answer: Brainstorming is a structured creativity technique where a group generates as many ideas as possible around a problem without immediate criticism. The conditions that make brainstorming most effective are: criticism is minimized (no negative evaluation during the session) freewheeling and bold ideas are encouraged (even wild suggestions are welcomed) the pace is quick and idea flow is high (quantity is valued over quality initially) and building on each other's ideas is allowed. All of these conditions together create the optimal brainstorming environment.

question: What is feasibility analysis and when should it be conducted?
gold_answer: Feasibility analysis is a preliminary evaluation of a business idea to determine whether it is viable before significant resources are committed. It is best conducted early in the planning stage — before major investment of time money or effort — to avoid pursuing an idea that the market does not support. A well-conducted feasibility analysis has four components and if the idea passes the analysis the logical next step is to write a full business plan.

question: Describe the four components of feasibility analysis.
gold_answer: Feasibility analysis has four components: Product/Service Feasibility which examines product desirability (whether consumers find the idea fundamentally appealing) and product demand (whether there is sufficient market demand). Industry/Target Market Feasibility which assesses the attractiveness of the industry (young fragmented growing industries are preferable) and the attractiveness of the target market (large enough to sustain the business but small enough to avoid dominant competitors). Organisational Feasibility which evaluates management prowess (the founder's passion knowledge and capabilities) and resource sufficiency (availability of critical non-financial resources like office space staff and IP protection). Financial Feasibility which considers total start-up cash needed financial performance of similar businesses and overall financial attractiveness of the proposed venture.

question: What is a concept statement and what is its purpose in product/service feasibility analysis?
gold_answer: A concept statement is a one-page summary of a business idea prepared to get feedback from potential customers and other stakeholders before significant resources are invested. It describes the product or service the target customer the problem being solved and why the proposed solution is superior to existing alternatives. It is NOT two to three pages — a concept statement should be concise (one page) so it is easy for respondents to review and comment on quickly.

question: What is the Bird-in-Hand Principle in effectuation and how does it differ from the Affordable Loss Principle?
gold_answer: The Bird-in-Hand Principle is an effectuation principle stating that entrepreneurs should start with what they already have — their existing skills knowledge networks and resources — rather than beginning with a desired end goal and trying to acquire what is needed. Esi Asante exemplifies this by starting her restaurant using her cooking skills blog audience and family farm produce. The Affordable Loss Principle is different: it focuses on evaluating opportunities based on whether the downside risk is acceptable rather than on the attractiveness of the predicted upside. Kwame exemplifies this by using personal savings and a simple prototype to limit potential losses rather than seeking large external funding.

question: What are the Patchwork Quilt Principle and the Lemonade Principle in effectuation?
gold_answer: The Patchwork Quilt Principle holds that entrepreneurs should build their venture collaboratively by enlisting partners stakeholders and co-creators — each partner brings resources commitments and capabilities that help shape and expand the venture. Akua Mensah demonstrates this by partnering with local seamstresses kente weavers and fabric traders. The Lemonade Principle holds that entrepreneurs should treat unexpected events and surprises as opportunities rather than as setbacks — turning lemons into lemonade. Yaw Owusu demonstrates this by pivoting to virtual fitness classes when COVID-19 disrupted in-person services expanding his reach significantly.

question: What is the Pilot-in-the-Plane Principle?
gold_answer: The Pilot-in-the-Plane Principle is an effectuation principle stating that entrepreneurs should focus on what they can control and actively shape their own future rather than merely reacting to external trends or forces. Instead of relying on prediction the effectual entrepreneur acts with the belief that the future is not fixed and can be constructed through their own decisions and commitments. Ama Nyarko demonstrates this by focusing on what she could control — quality brand values and ethical sourcing — and using that discipline to build a loyal customer base.

question: What is a business plan and what are the two main reasons entrepreneurs write them?
gold_answer: A business plan is the foundation of every new venture — a written document that carefully describes every aspect of the business turning concepts into a concrete roadmap for execution. The two main reasons entrepreneurs write business plans are: it forces the founding team to systematically think through every aspect of the new venture (revealing weaknesses and gaps before launch) and it serves as a document that communicates the merits of the new venture to outsiders such as investors and bankers who need to evaluate the opportunity before committing funds.

question: What are the three types of business plans and when is each appropriate?
gold_answer: The three types of business plans are: Summary Business Plan (10–15 pages) which works best for new ventures in the early stages of development that want to test the waters to see if investors are interested — suitable for high-profile entrepreneurs gauging early investor reaction. Full Business Plan (25–35 pages) which is the conventional complete plan used to raise funding and guide the business — presented to serious investors and lenders. Operational Business Plan which is primarily an internal document used to guide day-to-day operations and management decisions rather than for external fundraising.

question: What is the executive summary and why is it considered the most important section of a business plan?
gold_answer: The executive summary is a concise overview of the entire business plan — it should be a maximum of two pages. It is arguably the most important section because investors often decide from reading the executive summary alone whether to continue reading the full plan. A weak executive summary may cause an investor to discard the plan entirely without reviewing the detailed analysis and financial projections it contains. It must therefore clearly and compellingly convey the opportunity the solution the market and the team.

question: What does the industry analysis section of a business plan include?
gold_answer: The industry analysis section of a business plan describes the broader industry in which the venture will compete. It typically includes: the size of the industry its growth rate its structure (fragmented or concentrated) and key trends (technological social regulatory economic) that are shaping the industry. It helps investors and the founding team understand whether the industry context is favourable and whether the venture is entering at the right time.

question: What does the operations plan in a business plan describe?
gold_answer: The operations plan describes how the company will be run on a day-to-day basis — it is the section that holds the key to how the company will function. It covers both backstage activities (internal processes such as supply chain management manufacturing quality control and administration) and frontstage activities (customer-facing processes such as sales service delivery and customer support). It also describes the facilities and equipment the business will require to operate.

question: What does an attractive industry look like and what does Porter's Five Forces model assess?
gold_answer: An attractive industry for a new venture is typically young (early in the life cycle) fragmented (no single dominant player) and experiencing growth. Porter's Five Forces model assesses the competitive intensity and profitability potential of an industry by examining: the threat of new entrants (more entrants make competition harder) the bargaining power of suppliers (higher supplier power reduces firm profitability) the bargaining power of buyers (higher buyer power reduces pricing flexibility) the threat of substitute products (more substitutes reduce the firm's market power) and the intensity of rivalry among existing competitors (more rivals reduce profitability chances). A highly mature concentrated industry with slow growth expensive inputs and strong incumbents is highly unattractive for a new entrant.

question: What is a competitive analysis grid and what is a non-traditional barrier to entry?
gold_answer: A competitive analysis grid is a tool used in the market analysis section of a business plan that organises data about competitors to help the firm identify gaps and competitive advantages relative to existing players. A non-traditional barrier to entry is a unique operational model business model or way of doing business that becomes hard for others to replicate — as opposed to traditional barriers like capital requirements or government regulation. For example a startup that introduces a disruptive service model that transforms customer expectations creates a non-traditional barrier.

question: What are the four forms of intellectual property protection available to entrepreneurs?
gold_answer: The four main forms of intellectual property protection are: Patents which protect novel inventions and give the holder exclusive rights to make use and sell the invention for a defined period (Utility Patent: 20 years Design Patent: 14 years in Ghana). Trademarks which protect names logos symbols and sounds that distinguish a firm's products or services — they are renewable every 10 years. Copyrights which protect original creative works such as books music films and software — they generally last for the author's lifetime plus 70 years. Trade Secrets which protect confidential business information (formulas processes designs) that provide a competitive advantage through strict confidentiality measures like NDAs — they have no registration requirement and last indefinitely as long as the secret is maintained.

question: What are the steps involved in obtaining a trademark in Ghana?
gold_answer: The trademark registration process involves: conducting a Preliminary Search (optional) to check if similar marks already exist. Filing an Application (Form TM No. 2) with the relevant intellectual property office. Publication and Opposition (a 2-month window during which third parties can oppose the registration). Certification (issuance of the certificate if no successful opposition is filed). Note that PCT National Phase Filing is a step in patent registration not trademark registration.

question: How does copyright registration work in Ghana?
gold_answer: After submitting an application for copyright registration the Copyright Office determines within two weeks whether the work is a subject matter for registration and in writing informs the applicant accordingly. If the work qualifies the Copyright Office issues a certificate of registration of copyright or related right to the applicant within two weeks after informing the applicant that the work is a subject matter for registration. A copyright protects the expression of ideas (written works music films software artworks) but not the ideas themselves.

question: What is a trade secret and how does it differ from a patent?
gold_answer: A trade secret is confidential business information — such as a formula recipe process or method — that provides a competitive advantage and is protected by keeping it secret rather than by registration. Trade secrets are not known outside the company are known internally only on a need-to-know basis are safeguarded by stringent confidentiality measures (NDAs employment contracts) and last indefinitely as long as secrecy is maintained. A patent on the other hand is registered publicly grants exclusive rights for a fixed period and requires full public disclosure of the invention in exchange for that protection. A trade secret is never registered with the Copyright Office.

question: What are the three types of franchising arrangements?
gold_answer: The three types of franchising arrangements are: Individual Franchise Agreement which involves the sale of a single franchise for a specific location — the franchisor grants one franchisee the right to operate in one place. Area Franchise Agreement which allows a franchisee to own and operate a specific number of franchises in a particular geographic area. Master Franchise Agreement which gives the franchisee both the right to operate franchises in a geographic area AND the right to sell franchises to others (sub-franchisees) — the master franchisee essentially acts as a mini-franchisor within the territory.

question: What is the difference between a product distribution franchise and a business format franchise?
gold_answer: A product distribution franchise grants the franchisee the right to use the franchisor's trademark and sell its products but provides limited operational support — the focus is on product distribution (e.g. CarPro auto parts). A business format franchise grants not only the brand name but also provides the franchisee with a complete business system including training marketing support detailed operations manuals and ongoing support — the franchisee gets an entire way of running the business (e.g. Brew Bliss coffee shops KFC McDonald's).

question: What are the advantages of franchising for the franchisor and the franchisee?
gold_answer: For the franchisor the advantages include: reduced financial risk and investment burden (franchisees fund their own units) rapid expansion using local entrepreneurs' market knowledge and capital access to motivated local operators who have personal financial stakes in success and access to local knowledge that helps adapt the brand to regional consumer preferences and regulations. For the franchisee the advantages include: access to an established brand with proven systems and customer recognition reduced start-up risk (the business model is tested) training and ongoing support from the franchisor and lower failure rates compared to independent start-ups. Note that full control over all local operations is NOT an advantage for franchisors since franchisees operate independently.

question: What steps should a prospective franchisee follow before buying a franchise?
gold_answer: A prospective franchisee should follow these steps: conduct thorough research on the franchise opportunity and the industry. Carefully study the franchise disclosure document provided by the franchisor. Visit several of the franchisor's existing outlets to observe operations first-hand. Meet with the franchisor and its team to assess the relationship and support offered. Speak with existing franchisees to check their experiences and satisfaction. Check references thoroughly. Consult a franchise attorney and financial advisor before signing. Then open the franchise business with a clear operational understanding.

question: What are the three main sources of funding for new ventures and what type of venture suits each?
gold_answer: New ventures can be funded from three main sources matched to the venture's risk and growth profile: Personal funds friends and family and bootstrapping are most appropriate for high-risk ventures with uncertain returns weak cash flow and unproven management — when external funders are unlikely to be interested. Debt financing (bank loans SBA loans) is appropriate for lower-risk ventures with strong cash flow low leverage audited financials good management and a healthy balance sheet — lenders need predictable repayment. Equity financing (angel investors venture capital IPO) is appropriate for ventures offering high returns — they must have a unique business idea high growth potential a niche market and proven management.

question: What is bootstrapping and what are common examples of bootstrapping techniques?
gold_answer: Bootstrapping means using creative and resourceful methods to reduce costs and minimise dependence on external funding — building the business from within existing means. Common bootstrapping techniques include: buying used or second-hand equipment instead of new leasing assets rather than purchasing them outright requesting advance payments from customers to generate early cash flow sharing office space or resources with other businesses minimising personal drawings and reinvesting all early profits and leveraging sweat equity — the founder's time and effort — as a substitute for paid labour.

question: What is computer cracking and why is it a crime regardless of the cracker's motivation?
gold_answer: Computer cracking is the term for illegally hacking into a computer system without the permission of the system's owner. Regardless of the motivations of the computer cracker — whether curiosity financial gain patriotism or revenge — cracking a system is a crime. The intent does not matter under the law; the unauthorized access itself constitutes the illegal act.

question: Describe the White Hat Black Hat and Gray Hat hacker categories.
gold_answer: The White Hat/Black Hat model categorises hackers based on intent and legality. White hats represent the good guys — security professionals who use hacking skills ethically and legally to improve security. Black hats represent the bad guys — malicious hackers who break into systems illegally and without authorisation. Gray hat hackers occupy a middle ground — they may break into systems without permission but typically without malicious intent — demonstrating that the binary good/evil dichotomy is not a good fit for the real world.

question: What are the common motivations behind hacking?
gold_answer: The common motivations that drive hackers include: Curiosity and love of puzzles Desire for recognition or fame Revenge Financial gain Patriotism or politics. These motivations explain why the hacker community is diverse — not all hackers are motivated by malice or financial gain.

question: What is an ethical hacker and what is their role in information security?
gold_answer: An ethical hacker is a security professional who applies their hacking skills for defensive purposes. Ethics are the principles of conduct that govern individuals groups and professions. Some companies prefer to pay an ethical hacker to discover their systems' weaknesses and security gaps rather than wait for a malicious attacker to find them. Ethical hackers work to protect all areas of information technology and must have experience in software engineering network engineering and system security.

question: Describe the evolution of hacking from the 1950s to the 1990s.
gold_answer: The modern concept of hacking began in the late 1950s when students at MIT started using their access to the mainframe to work on new languages. The first password hacks were a response to the Compatible Time Sharing System (CTSS) developed in the early 1960s. In the 1970s phone phreaks used phreaking to make free calls from payphones by exploiting telephone networks. In the 1980s war dialers were developed to search for open modems personal computer prices dropped hacker communities grew and viruses worms and Trojans started appearing in 1988. The antisocial actions of crackers and script kiddies eventually led the term computer hacker to become associated with malicious intent rather than its original meaning of technical exploration.

question: What is reconnaissance in the context of penetration testing and what makes an activity legal versus illegal?
gold_answer: Reconnaissance is the act of locating targets and developing the methods necessary to attack those targets successfully. Reconnaissance is not by definition illegal — many techniques are completely legal. Legal activities include: looking up publicly available company information on the Internet calling for customer service assistance interviewing staff or attending facility tours. Questionable activities include: performing a passive port scan reading mail cart names war driving and looking through garbage cans. Illegal activities include: developing a front company for fraud stealing garbage entering a premises without authorisation dropping a keylogger and leaving a sniffer.

question: What is social engineering and what techniques do social engineers use?
gold_answer: Social engineering works because people are trusting and helpful — the weakest link in any security scheme is the user. Success depends on the ability of hackers to manipulate human psychology contacts and physical workstations. Common techniques include: Impersonation (pretending to be a person or service role) Bribery (exploiting greed and ignorance) Deception (joining a company as an employee or consultant) Conformity (building a fake rapport as a trusted friend) Phishing (tricking users into giving private account information) Reverse social engineering (projecting authority to get people to bring problems to the hacker) and Physical intrusion (entering a facility using fake identification after baselining its security procedures).

question: What is dumpster diving and why is it a significant security concern?
gold_answer: Dumpster diving is the practice of searching through an organisation's discarded trash to find sensitive information. It is often a mother lode of useful data including sales receipts and paperwork containing personal data or credit card information company directories policy manuals and catalog lists. Shredded documents can still lead to data leaks and drafts of letters are routinely left whole in the trash. Security policy must carefully address what constitutes sensitive information and decide how to treat refuse — the best solution is to use secure shredding methods for all sensitive paper waste.

question: What are the steps to counter social engineering attempts?
gold_answer: Steps to counter social engineering include: Never provide any information to unknown people. Never disclose confidential information over the telephone. Never type passwords or other confidential information in front of unknown people. Never submit information to insecure websites. Never use the same username and password across all accounts. Always verify credentials of persons asking for passwords. Keep confidential documents locked. Lock or shut down computers when away from the workstation. Instruct help desk employees to provide information only after gaining proper authentication from the requester.

question: What is a network scanner and how did scanners evolve historically?
gold_answer: A scanner is a software tool that examines and reports about vulnerabilities on local and remote hosts — it finds and helps fix vulnerabilities in remote machines on a network. A port scanner specifically examines and reports the condition (open or closed) of a port and the application listening on it. Scanners first appeared even before ARPANET to monitor connections between mainframes and dumb terminals. The Internet launched in the 1970s with no security. Early UNIX servers led to war dialers — scripts that dial a range of phone numbers to identify computers. In the early 1980s system administrators created shell scripts to check network security. As the Internet grew more scanners were developed for multiple platforms.

question: How do scanners work and what are the main types of scanning?
gold_answer: Scanners automate the process of examining network weaknesses. They are not heuristic (they do not learn). Their functions are: connect to a target host examine the target for services running on it and examine each service for known vulnerabilities. Main types of scanning include: TCP Connect Scanning (attempts TCP connections with all ports — no root needed but IDSs recognise it) Half-Open Scanning (sends only SYN — does not complete connections — requires root privileges) UDP Scanning (sends 0-byte UDP packets — ICMP unreachable reply indicates closed port) IP Protocol Scanning (examines supported protocols via ICMP unreachable replies) Ping Scanning (ICMP echo requests to check if host is active) and Stealth Scanning (examines hosts behind firewalls without being logged by the target).

question: Describe Nmap and its key advantages as a scanning tool.
gold_answer: Nmap (Network Mapper) is probably the best all-around network scanner available. It is powerful yet easy to use and supports many different operating systems. Its advantages include: Flexible (supports many scan types and protocols) Powerful (comprehensive scanning capabilities) Portable (runs on many platforms) Easy (simple command-line interface) Free (no cost) Well documented Supported Acclaimed and Popular. Basic Nmap commands in Red Hat Linux include: rpm -q nmap (check installation) nmap -A 192.168.0.1 (simple scan with OS detection and version detection) and nmap -A -P0 192.168.0.1 (scan without ping first).

question: What is a sniffer and what are the three categories of sniffers?
gold_answer: A sniffer (or packet sniffer) is an application that monitors filters and captures data packets transferred over a network. Sniffers are nearly impossible to detect in operation and can be implemented from almost any computer. The three types are: Bundled sniffers (come pre-installed with specific operating systems — e.g. Network Monitor on Windows tcpdump on Linux/UNIX Snoop on Solaris and nettl/netfmt on HP-UX) Commercial sniffers (used by companies to detect network problems — both fault analysis and performance analysis) and Free sniffers (used for the same purposes as commercial sniffers but with minimal support).

question: What are the components of a sniffer and how does it operate?
gold_answer: The main components of a sniffer are: Hardware (primarily the NIC) Capture Driver (captures network traffic from the Ethernet connection filters unwanted data and stores filtered traffic in a buffer) Buffer (a dynamic area of RAM that holds captured data — using either store-until-full or round-robin method) Decoder (interprets binary information and displays it in a readable format) and Packet Analysis (provides real-time analysis of captured packets). A sniffer must work with the type of network interface supported by the operating system and can only read traffic passing through the network interface adapter on the machine where it is installed.

question: What is promiscuous mode and how does it enable sniffing?
gold_answer: Promiscuous mode is a setting on a NIC that allows it to retrieve any data packet being transferred throughout an Ethernet network segment — not just packets addressed to that particular machine. A sniffer puts a network card into promiscuous mode using a programmatic interface that can bypass the TCP/IP stack of the operating system. In normal operation every adapter compares the destination MAC address in a received frame with its own MAC address and discards frames not addressed to it. In promiscuous mode this filtering is disabled so the sniffer can record all traffic on the network segment.

question: What is TCP/IP and how does the three-way handshake work?
gold_answer: TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) is a suite of protocols that underlie the Internet — the common language of networked computers. IP transmits data from source to destination and routes packets over network hardware but is connectionless (no guarantee of delivery). TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees delivery and correct ordering of packets using sequence numbers. The three-way handshake establishes a TCP connection: (1) Source sends a SYN packet with an Initial Sequence Number (ISN) (2) Destination replies with a SYN/ACK packet (3) Source sends an ACK to complete the connection. Connection release uses: FIN → FIN/ACK → ACK or an RST to immediately reset the session.

question: What is data encapsulation in TCP/IP and what are the key vulnerabilities in TCP/IP?
gold_answer: Data encapsulation is the process of enclosing higher-level protocol information in lower-level protocol information — also called data hiding. Key TCP/IP vulnerabilities include: IP Spoofing (attackers send packets with a false source address and must guess sequence numbers to maintain the connection) Connection hijacking (taking over an authenticated session) ICMP attacks Denial-of-Service attacks via TCP SYN flooding (flooding the network with SYN packets to exhaust resources) and RIP attacks. During TCP/IP's development in the 1980s security was not a priority — it was designed for a trusted academic environment making it inherently vulnerable to these attacks.

question: What are the TCP timers and what role do they play in TCP sessions?
gold_answer: All TCP sessions are tracked with timers built into the TCP protocol. The key timers are: Connection Establishment timer — a session will not be established if the destination server takes longer than 75 seconds to respond. FIN_WAIT timer — waits for FIN packets with a default value of 10 minutes. TIME_WAIT timer — default value of two minutes — waits for late packets to arrive at the destination. KEEP_ALIVE timer — checks whether the destination computer is still active by sending a test packet approximately every two hours to verify the other computer is alive and idle. These timers ensure sessions do not remain open indefinitely and that resources are properly released.

question: What is IP spoofing and what are the steps involved in a successful IP spoofing attack?
gold_answer: IP spoofing consists of a hacker accessing a target disguised as a trusted third party. The steps to perform an IP spoofing attack on a trusted machine relationship are: (1) Identify the target pair of trusted machines. (2) Anesthetize (stun/disable) the host the attacker intends to impersonate — typically using a SYN flood Ping of Death or other denial-of-service attack. (3) Forge the IP address of the stunned host. (4) Connect to the target machine as the assumed identity. (5) Accurately guess the correct TCP sequence number to complete the handshake — ISNs are not truly random and increment by fixed values making prediction possible. When the attack is complete the trusted machine must be released and returned to normal.

question: Describe the main types of spoofing attacks.
gold_answer: The main categories of spoofing attacks are: Blind Spoofing — the hacker can only see one side of the relationship and must guess responses without seeing the target's replies. Active Spoofing — the hacker can see both parties observe responses and perform various exploits such as sniffing data corrupting data or deleting packets. IP Spoofing — accessing a target disguised as a trusted third party. ARP Spoofing — modifying the ARP table by responding to ARP broadcast requests with the hacker's own MAC address redirecting traffic. Web Spoofing — spoofing a website's IP to intercept all communication between the site and the user. DNS Spoofing — changing a website's DNS record to point to the hacker's IP address directing users to the hacker's machine unknowingly.

question: What is session hijacking and how does TCP session hijacking work?
gold_answer: Session hijacking is when a hacker takes control of a TCP session between two hosts. A TCP session can only be hijacked after the hosts have authenticated successfully — the session cannot be initiated until authentication is complete. From the hacker's perspective: TCP tracks packets sent between machines. One method is using source-routed IP packets. If source routing is turned off the hacker uses blind hijacking — guessing the responses of the two machines. The hacker can also sit inline between the two hosts using a sniffer. A key problem is the ACK storm — the hijacked host and recipient continue sending ACKs creating a flood of traffic. Three ways to stop an ACK storm are: losing the ACK packet ending the connection or resynchronising the client and server.

question: How does route table modification enable session hijacking?
gold_answer: All computers using TCP/IP maintain a route table that shows the path to a destination IP address or the nearest source that might know the address. The route table has two sections: active routes and active connections. In route table modification a hacker changes the route table so the host computer assumes the best path for data transfer goes through the hacker's computer. Hackers can modify the route table by: (1) Erasing all necessary records from the route table and providing the hacker's own IP address as the default gateway or (2) Changing the corresponding route in the route table of the gateway router. This redirects all traffic through the attacker's machine enabling interception.

question: What is UDP hijacking and how does it differ from TCP session hijacking?
gold_answer: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a connectionless protocol that runs on top of IP networks providing very few error recovery services. It offers a direct way to send and receive datagrams over an IP network and is used primarily for broadcasting messages. UDP hijacking is more vulnerable to attack than TCP because UDP has no handshake or sequence numbers. The hacker needs only to sniff the network for a UDP request for a website and drop a spoofed UDP packet before the web server responds — there is no authentication or sequence number guessing required. This makes UDP sessions significantly easier to hijack than TCP sessions.

question: What are the defences against session hijacking?
gold_answer: The primary defences against session hijacking are: Encryption — using encrypted protocols makes it far too complicated and time-consuming for a hacker to get authenticated to intercept a session. Standard protocols like POP3 Telnet IMAP and SMTP are excellent targets for hijacking because they transfer data as plaintext — encrypted alternatives should be used instead. Storm Watching — setting an IDS rule to watch for abnormal increases in network traffic and alerting the security officer when they occur. An unexpected traffic increase could indicate an ACK storm. Packets with the same header information but different sizes could indicate a hijacking in progress.

question: What are the functions and vulnerabilities of proxy servers?
gold_answer: Proxy servers perform the following functions: restrict users from accessing specific websites using access rules mask the IP addresses of internal users from outside connections maintain logs of requests and user details and maintain a cache of visited sites. A proxy server is simple to install (often part of the server OS or included in router and firewall software) and the user is hidden — but can be traced through the proxy server's logs. Attacks on proxy servers fall into two groups: attacks made upon proxy servers directly and attacks made through proxy servers (including buffer overflow attacks denial-of-service attacks and session-hijacking attacks). Hackers exploit proxies by using chains of proxy servers or by spoofing valid authentication details to hide their identity.

question: What are the vulnerabilities of routers and switches and what attacks can be launched against them?
gold_answer: Routers and switches both segment a network and can filter packets but switches are considered to have lower security than routers since they are often viewed as internal network components. With VLAN technology some networks use gateway switches for logical network segmentation. If an attacker has access to the console port of a router they can easily set a remote user for the device. The default password for many Cisco routers is admin/admin. Common router attacks include: Denial-of-Service (DoS) Attack Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) Attack and Route Table Modification Attack. Hackers use port scans to discover open ports applications running on them and even the operating system of the target.

question: What are firewalls and what are their limitations?
gold_answer: Firewalls are often considered the ultimate one-point solution for securing networks from both internal and external threats. The main function of a firewall is to centralise access control by monitoring both inbound and outbound traffic and preventing unauthorised users and malicious code from entering a network. Firewalls are designed to be transparent to authorised users and intrusive to unauthorised users. Limitations include: limited ability to check data integrity cannot filter packets not sent through them firewalls from different vendors may not work well together do not provide robust application security do not stop all malicious code cannot detect attackers using valid credentials may miss attacks if not configured properly and are only effective if security policies are established and enforced.

question: What are the three methods of attacking a firewall?
gold_answer: Firewall attacks can be organised into three categories: Spoofing Session hijacking and Denial of service. The three basic methods to hack a firewall are: Back doors — an alternate method used to access a network after an initial attack — hackers may leave an alternate route back in. After an attack the computer should either be formatted and reinstalled or the specific bug used should be patched. Root access — used when hackers want to return to the network using root or administrator access — achieved by sniffing passwords through a back door or hijacking a session then installing a rootkit. Through the Web — since most firewalls permit access to remote web servers hackers can use search engines to find information about specific firewalls and exploit web-accessible services.

question: What is a Trojan horse how does it differ from viruses and worms and what are its typical functions?
gold_answer: A Trojan horse is an application that uses trickery to get a user to install it by masquerading as a legitimate useful program such as a game utility or software patch. Unlike viruses and worms Trojans cannot reproduce themselves — they must be installed by the user and activated. Typical Trojan functions include: logging keystrokes taking screen captures accessing files on local and shared drives acting as a server where the client is the hacker sending and receiving files viewing cached passwords restarting the system launching processes modifying files sharing files and modifying registry keys.

question: What are the main distribution vectors for Trojan horses and how can they be detected and prevented?
gold_answer: Trojan horses are distributed through: E-mail attachments Scripts in HTML emails Files on FTP servers Scripts on spoofed or hacked legitimate websites Download opportunities on websites Files on bulletin boards and forums and Social engineering. Recent attacks have disguised Trojans as patches — always validate checksums from legitimate download sites. Detection methods include: Object reconciliation (verifying date/time size and checksum of system files against originals) using MD5 Tripwire and other cryptographic checksum tools checking for unauthorised services and comparing system binaries to original installation files. Prevention best practices include: never open unverified executables never accept unexpected attachments never allow standard users to install programs install a software firewall and never run with root/administrator privileges.

question: Describe the famous Trojan horses in the history of cybersecurity.
gold_answer: Notable historical Trojan horses include: PC-Write (1986) — the first known Trojan masquerading as version 2.72 of the PC-Write shareware word processor — it wiped the FAT (file allocation table) and formatted the hard drive. AIDS.exe/PC Cyborg (1989) — distributed through postal mail claiming to contain AIDS/HIV information — the actual payload encrypted the hard drive and demanded a fee for the decryption password. Back Orifice (1998) — a remote administration server designed by the Cult of the Dead Cow allowing near-complete control of the victim machine — intentionally difficult to detect. Pretty Park (1999) — the first Trojan to use a worm for propagation — mailed itself to all addresses in the victim's address book and connected to IRC channels sending system information every 30 seconds. NetBus (2001) — allowed attackers to control the target with the same rights as the current user. SubSeven (1999) — enabled unauthorised access propagated via a forged Symantec email. BO2K — Back Orifice 2000 allowing infected machines to be used as a chain of proxy servers.

question: What are symmetric and asymmetric key encryption and how do they differ?
gold_answer: Symmetric key encryption (also called secret key algorithms) uses the same key to both encrypt and decrypt data. Both sender and recipient must have a copy of the key. The inherent vulnerability is that the key must be transmitted — if intercepted the encryption is broken. It is faster than asymmetric algorithms. Asymmetric key encryption (also called public key algorithms) uses two mathematically related keys: a public key and a private key. The public key can be distributed openly over unsecured media. The public key encrypts data and only the corresponding private key can decrypt it. This solves the key distribution problem of symmetric encryption but is slower.

question: Describe DES 3DES and AES — how do they work and how do they compare in security and speed?
gold_answer: DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a block cipher developed in the early-to-mid 1970s. It uses a 56-bit key breaks plaintext into 64-bit blocks and applies a series of permutations. It is FIPS-approved but susceptible to brute-force attacks due to its short key. 3DES (Triple DES) encrypts text three times with DES using different keys equivalent to a single DES with a 112-bit key but almost three times slower than DES. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard also known as Rijndael) superseded DES in 2001. It uses a 128-bit block size with 128- 192- or 256-bit keys. The input is copied to a 4×4 State array and transformed via substitutions and transpositions. AES is faster than DES but slower than Blowfish. All successful attacks on AES have been side-channel attacks (based on factors other than the algorithm's mathematical strength).

question: What is cryptography and what are the key terms associated with it?
gold_answer: Cryptography is the science of encrypting and decrypting information. An algorithm encrypts a plaintext document into ciphertext and decrypts it back. Key techniques include: Transposition (changing the position or order of letters — breakable by frequency analysis) and Substitution (replacing a letter or group of letters with another — the Enigma machine was a famous WWII substitution cipher broken by Alan Turing's Bombe machine). Key cryptographic terms are: Cleartext (unencrypted readable data) Ciphertext (encrypted data) Key (the value used by the algorithm to encrypt/decrypt) Algorithm (the mathematical procedure) and Hash (a fixed-size output derived from variable-length input — used to verify data integrity).

question: What is ARP spoofing how does it work and what is its relationship to session hijacking?
gold_answer: ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) spoofing involves modifying the ARP table for hacking purposes. The ARP table stores IP-to-MAC address mappings so routers can find the physical destination of a packet. In an ARP spoofing attack the hacker: detects ARP broadcast requests (when a host cannot find the MAC address for a destination IP it broadcasts an ARP request to the network) fakes the IP address of the legitimate destination and responds to the ARP request with the MAC address of the hacker's computer. This causes the ARP table of the requesting host to associate the target IP address with the hacker's MAC address redirecting all traffic intended for the target to the hacker's machine. ARP spoofing is a key method used by tools like Hunt to facilitate session hijacking.

question: What is Wireshark and what are its capabilities as a sniffer?
gold_answer: Wireshark (formerly known as Ethereal) is probably the best-known and most powerful free network protocol analyser available for UNIX/Linux and Windows. It allows users to capture packets from a live network in real time and save them to a capture file on disk. Data can be captured from a network connection directly or read from interfaces including Ethernet FDDI PPP token-ring and X.25. Wireshark provides real-time analysis and decoding of captured packets displaying them in human-readable format. It is widely used by both network administrators for legitimate monitoring and by penetration testers for security assessment.

question: What is a VPN and how does it provide secure remote access?
gold_answer: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) allows employees to access their company's network from a remote location using the Internet as a transport vehicle. VPNs use protocols like point-to-point tunneling to create an encrypted data tunnel over the public Internet. This means data transmitted between the remote user and the corporate network is encrypted making it unreadable to eavesdroppers on the Internet. VPNs are subject to their own vulnerabilities and can be attacked — the security of the VPN depends heavily on proper configuration the strength of the encryption protocols used and the security of the endpoints.

question: What are vendor-neutral security certifications available to computer security professionals?
gold_answer: Key vendor-neutral security certifications and their issuing bodies include: CompTIA Security+ Certification (CompTIA) Global Information Assurance Certification (GIAC) — Security Administration Certifications ISC2 Certifications including Associate of (ISC)2 SSCP (Systems Security Certified Practitioner) CAP (Certified Authorization Professional) CISSP (Certified Information Systems Security Professional) and CISSP Concentrations. EC-Council Certifications are also widely recognised. Additionally there are vendor-specific certificates such as Cisco's CCNA and Microsoft's MCSE which are useful to newcomers to the network security industry. There is currently no single national certification standard for computer security professionals.

question: What is the DNS spoofing attack and how does it redirect users to malicious sites?
gold_answer: DNS (Domain Name System) spoofing is an attack where the hacker changes a website's IP address in the DNS record to the IP address of the hacker's own computer. When a user tries to visit the legitimate website their DNS query returns the hacker's IP address instead. The user is then accessing the hacker's computer while believing they are accessing the legitimate site. This allows the hacker to: intercept all communication between the user and the apparent site steal login credentials and sensitive data serve malicious content or malware and harvest any information the user submits. DNS spoofing can be combined with web spoofing where the hacker ensures all communication between the spoofed website and the user passes through the hacker's computer.

question: What is IP fragmentation and why does it create a vulnerability?
gold_answer: When a large IP packet is sent over a network it is broken down into smaller pieces — this process is called fragmentation. IP packets often arrive out of sequence — a vulnerability that attackers can exploit. Attackers can craft fragmented IP packets that: reassemble into malicious payloads that bypass firewall inspection overlap with previous fragments to overwrite data and exploit weaknesses in how different operating systems reassemble fragments. Additionally IP is connectionless with no guarantee of delivery or correct ordering — this combined with the fragmentation mechanism means security devices must reconstruct entire packet streams to inspect payloads which is computationally expensive and can be exploited for evasion.

question: What is an expert system according to Professor Edward Feigenbaum?
gold_answer: According to Professor Edward Feigenbaum of Stanford University an expert system is a computer system that emulates or acts in all respects with the decision-making capabilities of a human expert. An expert system takes its roots in Cognitive Science and was among the first successful applications of AI to real-world problems. Expert systems are computer programs that try to replicate the knowledge and skills of human experts in some domain.
